Paper 3: The New Testament, Religion in Relation to Philosophy, Ethics and Morality, Historical Development of Islam (570CE-661CE). Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

The paper has six sections of six questions each: Section 2.1 The Gospel According to Luke (questions 1-6); Section 2.2 The Fourth Gospel (questions 7-12); Section 2.3 The Early Church as Reflected in Acts and 1 Corinthians (questions 13-18); Section 4.1 Philosophy of Religion (questions 19-24); Section 4.2 Ethics and Morality (questions 25-30); Section 6.0 The Historical Development of Islam (570CE - 661CE) (questions 31-36).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.corrige_markdown: Ali ibn Abi Talib was the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad and the fourth of the rightly guided caliphs. He was the son of Abu Talib, the Prophet's uncle and protector, and, according to tradition, was brought up in the Prophet's household. He was one of the first persons, and the first boy, to accept Islam. He slept in the Prophet's bed on the night of the Hijra to mislead those plotting against him, and he married the Prophet's daughter Fatima, by whom he was the father of Hasan and Husayn. He was a brave soldier at Badr, Uhud, the Trench and Khaybar, and was known for his learning, piety and justice. He became caliph in 656 after the assassination of Uthman, and was killed in 661 at Kufa by a Kharijite, Ibn Muljam. The Shi'a regard him as the first Imam.

questions.enonce_markdown:
How relevant was his rule during the Early Ummah?

(20 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The rule of Ali (656-661) was one of the most troubled periods of the early community, and it is highly relevant for the later history of Islam.

- *Beginning amid crisis.* Ali was chosen caliph in Medina after Uthman was killed by rebels from the provinces. His election was disputed, and his rule began in a climate of anger and division. He wished to restore order before dealing with the murderers of Uthman, while others demanded immediate punishment.
- *Reforms and policy.* He dismissed a number of governors appointed by Uthman, whom he regarded as unjust or unsuitable, and tried to apply equal treatment in the distribution of the public funds. He lived a simple life and was known for his concern for justice and the poor. This won him support but also made enemies among those who had lost their positions.
- *The first civil war (the first fitna).* Aisha, Talha and Zubayr demanded vengeance for Uthman and raised an army. Ali defeated them at the Battle of the Camel near Basra (656). Talha and Zubayr were killed, and Aisha was sent back to Medina with respect. This was the first time Muslims fought Muslims in large numbers.
- *Mu'awiya and Siffin.* Mu'awiya, the governor of Syria and a relative of Uthman, refused to recognise Ali until the killers of Uthman were punished. The armies met at Siffin (657). When Ali's side seemed to be winning, Mu'awiya's soldiers raised copies of the Qur'an on their spears and called for arbitration. Ali accepted it under pressure from his own army, but the arbitration was inconclusive.
- *The Kharijites.* A group in Ali's army objected to arbitration, saying that judgement belonged to God alone, and withdrew. They were the first sect in Islam, and they fought Ali at Nahrawan (658). Their later hostility led to his assassination.
- *Move to Kufa.* Ali moved his capital from Medina to Kufa in Iraq, which shifted the political centre of Islam away from the Hijaz and left Medina.
- *Division of the community.* His supporters, the party of Ali (*Shi'at Ali*), later grew into the Shi'a, who see him and his descendants as the rightful leaders. The Sunnis count him as the fourth rightly guided caliph. The disputes of his reign thus shaped the main divisions in Islam.
- *The end of the Rashidun period.* After his death in 661 his son Hasan gave up the caliphate, and Mu'awiya founded the Umayyad dynasty, which changed the character of the caliphate toward hereditary rule.
- *A model of justice and learning.* His sermons, sayings and judgements have been preserved and admired in both traditions as examples of wisdom and piety.

Ali's rule was therefore relevant as the time of the first major internal conflict, the beginning of lasting divisions, the end of the period of the first four caliphs and a source of moral example.
